newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan night-owl money trade thrives on margin.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan night-owl money trade thrives on margin.

text.p: When night falls and Taipei traffic slows to a snail's pace, some Taiwan currency dealers are just getting started -- firing off quotes and buy/sell orders from otherwise deserted trading rooms.
Round-the-clock margin trading is getting a boost this year as banks step up competition to tap growing customer interest in cross-currency business, banking sources say.

Margin currency trading, where investors put up a small amount of money -- a good faith deposit -- in order to trade several times the amount, was legalised in Taiwan in 1991 but has only recently begun to take off.
"Margin trading comes to life in the late afternoon hours when the London market opens," said one currency dealer. "The activity continues through the evening."
Taipei is eight hours ahead of London.

Morris Li, vice-president and emerging markets treasurer of Citibank's Taiwan office, said the island's relatively lackluster currency trading has prompted restless dealing managers to seek new business.

A stable U.S. dollar in the first half of 1996 cut profits from proprietary trading and a flat Taiwan dollar since the turbulence from China's military exercises peaked in March have further depressed business volumes, Li said.
At the same time, dwindling derivatives business has starved banks of revenue. Li said onerous new reporting requirements for firms using derivatives were hurting the young market.

Courted by solicitous banks, currency speculators are happy to switch from poorly-regulated "bucket shops" to trade through banks. Some dealers estimate the market is growing as much as 20 percent a month.

Margin transactions are all U.S. dollar-based against major trading currencies such as the German mark, Japanese yen, Swiss franc, Australian dollar and Canadian dollar. Daily trading volume has averaged about $100 million in recent months, according to a source at Taiwan's central bank.
Margin trading in the Taiwan dollar is prohibited and securities brokerages are not allowed to trade currencies.
Banks vary in initial margin requirements and leverage.
Citibank, for example, sets an initial margin at $100,000 which allows customers to trade up to $1 million.

With Standard Chartered Bank's Taiwan margin-trade operation, regular customers with a $25,000 good-faith deposit can trade 10 times the limit. For selected customers with "market savvy," a 20-times leverage is possible, said a dealer at the bank.
Under competitive pressure, some banks have gone out of their way to be flexible.
"Some foreign banks would not allow that extent of leverage in other markets, but they would do it in Taiwan for fear of losing to the competition," said a foreign bank dealer.
Foreign banks control the lion's share of margin accounts with domestic banks struggling to catch up, said Daniel Chen, chief economist at Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
"Foreign banks have an edge on us," Chen said. "They have always been more trading-oriented in the forex business."
The more conservative Taiwan banks are wary of the high leverage of margin trading, especially after highly-publicised derivatives losses, Chen said.
Margin trading is appropriate only for the investors who have a large capital cushion and a commitment to allocate a small portion of their assets to this high-risk high-return activity, Li noted.
Banks demand extra margin deposits in volatile markets and will close positions if these fail, he said.
